relations.evidence: To use the examples on this page, you must set the query context to the `inventory` scope in the travel sample dataset.

notable_absence.finding: Six absences, the first two of them serious. (1) No version information anywhere on the page, in a document whose prose is written as release notes: 'The Indexer has been enhanced to perform grouping, COUNT(), SUM(), MIN(), MAX(), AVG(), and related operations' and 'Currently, the only aggregate functions that are supported are ...' both invite the question 'since when?' and neither answers it. The only trace of a version is in image filenames - GBAP_Ex0_QP_before55.png, GBAP_Ex0_QP_after55.png, GBAP_55execution-*.svg and GBAP_pre55execution-*.svg - which date the feature to Couchbase Server 5.5. A reader of the rendered page cannot see those names; the version fact exists only in the asset paths. This is the mirror image of index-scans.md, whose only version fact is a stale 'In version 4.5' note. (2) No cost, and no way to turn the feature off. The page lists five benefits (improved query response time, improved resource utilization, low latency, high scalability, low TCO) and says 'Not every query will benefit from this optimization', but never says what the Indexer pays for doing the aggregation - no statement about indexer CPU or memory, no cardinality limit on the number of groups, no equivalent of index-scans.md's concrete 8192-element threshold, and no setting or hint that disables the pushdown if it turns out to be the wrong choice. There is no requiresSetting or hasDefaultValue relation to be had on this page at all: the feature is presented as unconditionally on and unconditionally good. (3) Nothing about partitioned indexes or index replicas. Aggregating inside the Indexer across a partitioned index requires the same partial-then-merge treatment the page describes for non-leading keys, and the word 'partition' does not appear. (4) No vector or full-text indexes, on an 8.0 page that otherwise enumerates index shapes (composite, array with DISTINCT, array with ALL, primary). (5) The interaction with ORDER BY is left unresolved: the Limitations list says 'ORDER BY clauses' are not pushed to the indexer, yet Examples 1, 2, 4, 15 and 16 all carry an ORDER BY and all still show index_group_aggs in the plan, and index_pushdowns.md documents a separate order pushdown. What happens when both are candidates is never said. (6) Broken and stale anchors, which matter because the page's own tables are cross-referenced by number: '[Table 3](#docs-internal-guid-facfdbc0-bb3d-b00f-2ec0-6bee4921dabc)' is a leftover Google Docs internal GUID, '[Example 15](#ex10)' still uses the anchor from when that example was numbered 10 (its image is GBAP_Ex10_VP.png), and '[Appendix: Query Plan Fields](#section%5Fbpf%5Fwjf%5Fycb)' and '[Table 2](#table%5Fbw2%5Fnrf%5Fycb)' are generated DITA ids. The page's authoring history is visible in its link targets.

cross_component_finding: This is the least internally consistent page in the batch: nine defects, several of them contradictions between the page's own sections. (a) ARRAY_AGG() is documented three times with three different answers. The positive-case list at the top includes `SELECT ARRAY_AGG(geo.alt) FROM airport WHERE geo.alt > 10;` under the heading 'Positive Case examples of queries that use indexing grouping and aggregation'; the Limitations list says '`ARRAY_AGG()` or any facility to add new Aggregate function, such as Median.' is not supported and not pushed to the indexer; and Table 1 marks 'Supports ARRAY_AGG()' as unsupported in all four columns. Two of the three must be wrong. (b) Table 1 (Aggregate Comparison) disagrees with the prose on its own subject. Its 'Supports SUM() and COUNT()' row is marked unsupported for 'Aggregate on Non-Array Index Field' - that is, the single most common case in the whole document, demonstrated by Examples 1, 2, 5, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 16, and contradicted by the sentence 'Currently, the only aggregate functions that are supported are SUM(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX(), and AVG() with or without the DISTINCT modifier.' The same row marks MIN()/MAX() unsupported for both DISTINCT columns. As printed, Table 1 cannot be used. (c) Two mutually exclusive failure modes. The Scenarios section promises silent degradation - 'When the requirements are unmet, the query will fetch the relevant data and then do the grouping and acceleration as usual. No application changes are necessary.' - while the DISTINCT section says 'All other cases of DISTINCT pushdown will return an error.' A query that fails to qualify either quietly runs slower or fails outright, depending on which paragraph you read. (d) The wrong component is named twice in one bullet list: 'The SQL++ indexer will do 2nd level of aggregation and compute the final result' and 'The SQL++ indexer can pushdown only if the leading key has a predicate.' Both jobs belong to the Query service (the second-level merge) and the optimizer (the pushdown decision); Example C's own prose says so - 'the indexer sends partial group aggregation, which the query merges to create the final group and aggregation.' 'SQL++ indexer' looks like a mechanical substitution into what was once 'N1QL engine'. (e) Example 4 does not demonstrate what its section claims. It sits under 'GROUP BY keys in different CREATE INDEX order', is introduced as 'Like Example 1 with the GROUP BY fields swapped', and uses index idx3 on (activity, city, geo.lon) - but its WHERE clause is `country IS NOT MISSING`, a predicate on a field that is not in idx3 at all. By the page's own rule ('1st index field must be in a WHERE clause'; 'Without a matching predicate, the query will use the primary index') the example cannot select idx3, let alone push the grouping down. No plan is shown, so the claim is unverifiable. (f) Example 6 is filed under the positive 'Syntax B: Operation on a field - GROUP BY and Index keys match', but its index idx4_oper is on (sourceairport, ROUND(distance*stops), distance) while the query groups by UPPER(sourceairport) - precisely the shape the page labels 'Pre-aggregated Syntax - the GROUP BY and Index keys don't match' three paragraphs earlier. Again no plan is shown. (g) Example 3 gives no index at all and groups by ROUND(geo.lat) against idx1 (country, state, geo.lat), so it too is a pre-aggregated case presented among the positive ones, and its narrative reason for using MIN() ('At a particular latitude, the state will be the same; but an aggregate function on it is needed') is a data assumption that the sample data does not guarantee. (h) The FILTER-clause workaround does not match its own description: the prose says 'you can use a comparison operator as the argument for the aggregate function', and the example then uses CASE WHEN expressions, not comparison operators. (i) The four DISTINCT cases are stated twice, and the two statements do not agree word for word: the numbered list at the head of the section reads 'If the DISTINCT aggregate is on the leading GROUP By key(s) + 1 (the immediate next key).' - with 'GROUP By' mis-capitalised - while the Case 2 heading reads 'If the DISTINCT aggregate is on the leading GROUP BY key(s) + 1 (the next key).' The write-time evidence gate caught this: my first attempt at the record quoted a conflation of the two, which is exactly the fabrication the gate exists to stop, and the fix was to re-read and quote the Case 2 heading. Two further structural observations. The feature is named four ways in one document - 'Grouping and Aggregate Pushdowns' (title), 'grouping and aggregate pushdown' (Overview), 'Aggregate Pushdown' (every syntax heading, including the GROUP BY-only sections) and 'Index Aggregations' (appendix callout) - and the components are named 'indexer', 'Indexer', 'query engine', 'query', 'SQL++ indexer' and 'data service (KV service)'. And the same eleven-row field-description table is printed three times (appendix, Table 2, Table 3) with identical Description text and only the example column differing; Table 3 repeats its '... depends / ... expr / ... id / ... keypos' rows twice to cover two group keys, giving fifteen rows. Roughly 200 of the page's 2168 lines are that one table. Finally, the module's link topology, since this page completes the set: this page, index_pushdowns.md and covering-indexes.md each end with a Related Links list naming the other four siblings; early-filters-and-pagination.md names the four siblings plus WHERE, ORDER BY, OFFSET and LIMIT in the language reference (seven links); and index-scans.md has no Related Links section at all, although all four of the others link into its #query-execution-details anchor. This corrects the wording of this round's index-scans.json record, which described the sibling lists as 'four items' each - early-filters-and-pagination.md has seven.
cross_product_finding: Two findings, one about naming and one about the storage question this batch was asked to watch. (1) This single page's subject now carries five ids in the extraction layer, one per copy or per audience: `index:group-aggregate-pushdown` (37 occurrences - the most heavily attested unpromoted concept I met anywhere in this batch, and the one I reused), `n1ql:groupby-aggregate-performance`, `learn:grouping-and-aggregate-pushdown`, `page:groupby-aggregate-performance` and `guides:group-agg`. The last of those is worth phase 2's attention because cloud/guides/group-agg.json is not a copy of this page at all - it is a separate Capella guide about the same feature, so the concept is documented in three products and at least four page shapes (server reference, Capella reference, Capella guide, SQL++ language reference GROUP BY page). `index:partial-aggregation` already existed from the Capella copy, which is why I reused rather than minted it. As with index-scans.md, the fact that one concept is documented four times will make recurrence counting read the best-attested term in the module as several weak ones unless aliases are resolved before counting. Also visible while I was checking ids: concurrently running agents have just minted `index:span-inclusion-enum`, `index:exact-index-span`, `index:full-scan` and `index:skip-key-range-scan` alongside my `index:span-inclusion`, `index:exact-span`, `index:full-index-scan` and `n1ql:skip-key-range-scan` - four more alias pairs created in the same round, exactly as expected. (2) On storage engines versus storage modes, this page is the clearest single piece of evidence that the ambiguity is in the source, not in the registry. It says 'Grouping and aggregate pushdown is supported on both storage engines: Standard GSI and Memory Optimized GSI (MOI)' - calling the two user-selectable index storage MODES 'engines', where the registry has them promoted as index:standard-storage and index:memory-optimized-storage. It names no actual engine: Plasma, Forestdb and Nitro do not appear on this page, nor on any of the other four pages in my batch. Meanwhile the extraction layer has acquired `storage-engine:plasma` and `storage-engine:forestdb` from other agents working on the storage-modes and buckets pages, while concepts/storage-engine/ holds only couchstore and magma - so the KV engines are promoted, the index engines are attested but not promoted, and the one sentence in the performance documentation that mentions 'storage engines' actually means modes. Phase 2 should treat 'storage engine' in indexing prose as unreliable and prefer the mode ids unless an engine is named.
